mcqs.question: Why is the main queue specifically a serial queue rather than a concurrent one?
options: So UI updates never race against each other, since only one task runs on it at a time
So multiple UI updates can be applied simultaneously for better performance
Serial queues use less memory than concurrent queues
It's an arbitrary default with no functional reason
mcqs.explanation: A serial queue guarantees only one task executes at a time, in order — exactly the property UIKit and SwiftUI need so that concurrent UI mutations can't corrupt view state. A concurrent main queue would reintroduce the exact race conditions the serial guarantee prevents.

mcqs.question: Besides readability, what's a concrete correctness advantage of async/await over three nested completion-handler closures?
options: async/await functions always execute faster than completion-handler equivalents
The compiler enforces that a suspension point resumes exactly once, preventing the 'forgot to call the completion handler' bug that plain closures allow
async/await eliminates the need for any error handling
Completion handlers cannot be used with network requests, only async/await can
mcqs.explanation: A recurring real bug with manual completion handlers is a code path that never calls the closure (an early return, a missed branch); async/await's compiler-checked suspension model doesn't allow that class of mistake. It doesn't guarantee faster execution, doesn't remove the need for try/catch, and completion handlers work fine for network requests — they're just more error-prone to chain.

mcqs.question: Two tasks call store(_:for:) concurrently on the same actor-based ImageCache. What prevents the underlying dictionary from being corrupted?
options: Dictionaries in Swift are inherently thread-safe for concurrent writes
The actor serializes access to its own state, so the two calls run one at a time rather than racing
Both calls run in parallel but on separate copies of the dictionary that get merged afterward
The compiler automatically wraps the actor's methods in a global lock shared across all actors
mcqs.explanation: An actor's defining guarantee is that its mutable state is only ever accessed by one task at a time, serializing concurrent calls rather than letting them race — that's what actor isolation actually enforces. Swift dictionaries are not inherently thread-safe, and there's no per-actor copy-and-merge or shared global lock involved.

mcqs.question: A button's @IBAction wraps an async call in Task { await fetchData() }. The view is dismissed while the fetch is still in flight. What happens to the task by default?
options: It continues running to completion regardless of the view's disappearance, unless explicitly stored and cancelled
It is automatically cancelled the instant the view disappears
It pauses and resumes automatically when the view reappears
The app crashes because the Task has no associated view to complete against
mcqs.explanation: A Task started this way is detached from the caller's UI lifetime by default and keeps running unless the code explicitly stores a reference and calls cancel(), commonly tied to onDisappear. There's no automatic cancellation or pause/resume tied to view lifecycle without that explicit wiring.

mcqs.question: How does marking a class @MainActor improve on the old GCD pattern of manually wrapping UI updates in DispatchQueue.main.async?
options: It has identical safety guarantees, just with less typing
It makes background threads execute faster when they eventually reach the UI update
The compiler can reject an attempt to touch the type's state off the main actor at compile time, rather than only failing at runtime like a missed manual dispatch
It removes the need for the UI update to ever run on the main thread at all
mcqs.explanation: @MainActor is a compile-time enforced guarantee, so an accidental off-main access is caught before the app ships rather than surfacing as an intermittent runtime bug from a forgotten DispatchQueue.main.async. It doesn't change the fact that UI work must run on main, and it doesn't inherently speed anything up.

mcqs.question: An actor's withdraw method checks a guard on balance, then awaits a logging call, then decrements balance. Two concurrent calls to withdraw both pass the guard before either decrements. What does this demonstrate?
options: This can't happen — actors fully serialize all method calls with no interleaving possible
The bug means the actor keyword wasn't applied correctly to the class
This only happens if the actor is marked @MainActor as well
Actors eliminate data races on raw memory access, but a suspension point (await) inside a method can still let a logic race happen between the check and the mutation
mcqs.explanation: Actors serialize direct memory access to their state, but an await point genuinely suspends the current call, letting another call run against the same actor in between — that's actor reentrancy, and it can create a logic race across the suspension even though no raw data race occurs. This isn't a misuse of actor; it's an inherent property that requires re-checking invariants after an await.
